claim: Protein synthesis consumes up to 50% of cellular energy in bacteria.
source: Protein synthesis is the most energetically costly process in bacteria, consuming up to 50% of cellular energy.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the introduction without specific citation, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The rate of protein production of adjacent ORFs on a single mRNA can vary by as much as 100-fold.
source: Indeed, the rate of protein production (i.e. the translation efficiency) of adjacent ORFs on a single mRNA can vary by as much as 100-fold, and members of protein complexes encoded on a single mRNA are generally translated in proportion to their stoichiometry (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Members of protein complexes encoded on a single mRNA are generally translated in proportion to their stoichiometry.
source: Indeed, the rate of protein production (i.e. the translation efficiency) of adjacent ORFs on a single mRNA can vary by as much as 100-fold, and members of protein complexes encoded on a single mRNA are generally translated in proportion to their stoichiometry (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Both the strength and accessibility of a Shine-Dalgarno sequence upstream from the initiation codon have been implicated in translatability.
source: Both the strength and accessibility of a Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence upstream from the initiation codon (Steitz and Jakes, 1975) have been implicated in translatability.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Steitz and Jakes, 1975.

claim: Highly stable mRNA structures in direct proximity to the initiation codon diminish translatability.
source: In support of the importance of SD accessibility, highly stable mRNA structures in direct proximity to the initiation codon diminish translatability (de Smit and van Duin, 1990; Hall et al., 1982; Lodish, 1970)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Smit and van Duin, 1990; Hall et al., 1982; Lodish, 1970.

claim: Rare codons that disfavor RNA structure are enriched in positions immediately following the translation start site.
source: and rare codons that disfavor RNA structure are enriched in positions immediately following the translation start site (Bentele et al., 2013; Eyre-Walker and Bulmer, 1993; Scharff et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bentele et al., 2013; Eyre-Walker and Bulmer, 1993; Scharff et al., 2011.

claim: A read coverage of ~15 reads/nucleotide is sufficient for reproducible structure determination in DMS-seq.
source: By exploring the effect of coverage on reproducibility, we find that a read coverage of ~15 reads/nucleotide is sufficient for reproducible structure determination (Figure 1B), and used this cutoff in all subsequent analyses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMS-seq structures determined from E. coli are in excellent agreement with the 16S rRNA crystal structure.
source: Structures determined from E. coli-adapted DMS-seq are in excellent agreement with both the 16S rRNA crystal structure (Figure 1C) (Zhang et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with crystal structure data (Zhang et al., 2009) and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DMS-seq structures are in excellent agreement with a mutationally verified E. coli mRNA structure.
source: and a mutationally verified E. coli mRNA structure (Figure 1D) (Wikström et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with mutationally verified structure (Wikström et al., 1992) and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Signal threshold of 0.2 has 90% agreement with the 16S rRNA crystal structure.
source: Signal threshold of 0.2 has 90% agreement with the crystal structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1C caption and supported by the ROC curve data shown in the figure.

claim: The degree of RNA secondary structure varies greatly between ORFs.
source: We found that the degree of RNA secondary structure varied greatly between ORFs: a small number are nearly as structured as rRNA, whereas some are close to the denatured state (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the histogram of Gini indices shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Individual ORFs generally have fairly consistent Gini scores across their bodies.
source: In contrast to the large variation in the degree of secondary structure among ORFs (Figure 1F), individual ORFs generally have fairly consistent Gini scores across their bodies – for example, the first and second halves of each ORF exhibit highly correlated Gini scores (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Gini scores across ORFs remain correlated in the absence of translation when translation initiation is inhibited with kasugamycin.
source: We tested whether the Gini scores across ORFs remained correlated in the absence of translation in two different conditions. First, we examined Gini scores of in vivo mRNA when translation initiation was inhibited with kasugamycin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from kasugamycin-treated cells.

claim: Gini scores across ORFs remain correlated when mRNA is purified and refolded in vitro at 37°C.
source: Second, we examined Gini scores of purified mRNA refolded in vitro at 37°C.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro refolded mRNA.

claim: Translation-independent mRNA structures obtained from DMS-seq indicate that Gini scores across the ORF mRNAs remain correlated.
source: In both cases, the translation-independent mRNA structures obtained from DMS-seq indicated that Gini scores across the ORF mRNAs remain correlated (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Computationally predicted mRNA structure of ORFs shows correlated Gini scores across the ORF.
source: This correlation also holds true for computationally predicted mRNA structure of ORFs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The degree of mRNA structures determined in various ways (in vivo, in vitro, kasugamycin-treated) are highly correlated with each other.
source: Moreover, the degree/extent of mRNA structures (henceforth referred to as structure) determined in these various ways are highly correlated with each other (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: mRNA is organized in ORF-wide structures that depend on the intrinsic sequence of the mRNA.
source: We conclude that mRNA is organized in ORF-wide structures that depend on the intrinsic sequence of the mRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation data across different conditions.

claim: Within operonic (polycistronic) mRNAs, the mRNA structure of adjacent ORFs can differ significantly.
source: Within operonic (polycistronic) mRNAs, the mRNA structure of adjacent ORFs can differ significantly (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Adjacent ORFs with overlapping start and stop codons can have significantly different mRNA structures.
source: even when the start and stop codons of the adjacent ORFs overlap (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Characteristic mRNA structures are a property of individual ORF mRNAs rather than of the entire polycistronic transcript.
source: Thus, characteristic mRNA structures are a property of individual ORF mRNAs rather than of the entire polycistronic transcript.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that adjacent ORFs have different structures.

claim: The TE's of E. coli endogenous ORFs in operonic mRNAs are highly negatively correlated with their level of ORF-wide mRNA structure (ρ = −0.75).
source: We found that the TE's of E. coli endogenous ORFs in operonic mRNAs were highly negatively correlated with their level of ORF-wide mRNA structure (ρ = −0.75, Figure 3A: well-translated ORFs have less mRNA structure, while poorly translated ORFs have more structure).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Well-translated ORFs have less mRNA structure, while poorly translated ORFs have more structure.
source: We found that the TE's of E. coli endogenous ORFs in operonic mRNAs were highly negatively correlated with their level of ORF-wide mRNA structure (ρ = −0.75, Figure 3A: well-translated ORFs have less mRNA structure, while poorly translated ORFs have more structure).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The TE's of adjacent ORFs can differ significantly.
source: Consistent with the fact that the ORF-wide mRNA structures of adjacent ORFs in an operon can differ significantly (Figure 2G), the TE's of adjacent ORFs can also differ significantly (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ORF pairs with overlapping start and stop codons show essentially as much variability in their relative translation as non-overlapping ORF pairs (p=0.06, K-S test).
source: Notably, ORF pairs with overlapping start and stop codons, believed to be translationally coupled (Aksoy et al., 1984; Oppenheim and Yanofsky, 1980; Schümperli et al., 1982; Yates and Nomura, 1981), show essentially as much variability in their relative translation as non-overlapping ORF pairs (p=0.06, K-S test, Figure 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (K-S test) and data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The extent of translational coupling between overlapping ORFs is variable.
source: suggesting that the extent of coupling is variable.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overlapping ORFs show similar variability in translation as non-overlapping ORFs.

claim: The level of mRNA structure and TE are highly anti-correlated on all endogenous open reading frames (ρ = −0.76).
source: We then expanded this analysis beyond operons to all ORFs and found that the level of mRNA structure and TE are highly anti-correlated on all endogenous open reading frames (ρ = −0.76, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gini scores calculated from control RNA samples without DMS modification are not correlated to TE (ρ = 0.05).
source: Importantly, the Gini scores of ORFs calculated from control RNA samples without DMS modification were not correlated to TE (ρ = 0.05, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by the control data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Gini scores calculated from DMS-seq reflect the level of mRNA structure and sequencing bias/noise does not contribute to the correlation between TE and mRNA structure.
source: indicating that Gini scores calculated from DMS-seq indeed reflect the level of mRNA structure and the potential sequencing bias/noise does not contribute to the correlation between TE and mRNA structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation in control samples without DMS modification.

claim: When translation is inhibited in vivo (kasugamycin treatment), the absolute correlation of TE to structure remains high but decreases somewhat (ρ = −0.58).
source: We find that when translation is inhibited in vivo (e.g. following kasugamycin treatment), the absolute correlation of TE to structure remains high but decreases somewhat (ρ = −0.58, Figure 3D)
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is a small further decrease in correlation when mRNAs are refolded in vitro (ρ = −0.48).
source: and that there is a small further decrease in correlation when mRNAs are refolded in vitro (ρ = −0.48, Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Computationally predicted structures of entire ORFs show robust correlation to their TE's (ρ = −0.52).
source: Additionally, computationally predicted structures of entire ORFs also show robust correlation to their TE's (ρ = −0.52, Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There is a tendency for mRNA to be more structured (higher Gini index) in the absence of translation.
source: We found that there is a tendency for mRNA to be more structured (higher Gini index) in the absence of translation (Figure 2E)
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: mRNAs with the highest TEs have the greatest difference in their Gini scores with and without translation (ρ = 0.52).
source: and that mRNAs with the highest TEs had the greatest difference in their Gini's (ρ = 0.52, Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Unwinding by ribosomes contributes to the in vivo structure of highly translated genes.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that unwinding by ribosomes contributes to the in vivo structure of highly translated genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that highly translated genes show greater structural differences with and without translation.

claim: The correlation of TE with extent of structure increases as successively larger regions of the ORF are considered in the structural analysis.
source: We find increasing correlation with TE as successively larger regions of the ORF are considered in the structural analysis (−20nt to 40nt, 0 to 60nt, and 0 to 100nt relative to the gene start).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The correlation of TE with extent of structure in either the first or second halves of the ORF are very similar.
source: Notably, the correlation of TE with extent of structure in either the first or second halves of the ORF are very similar
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The highest correlation of TE is with the Gini of the ORF-wide mRNA structure.
source: and the highest correlation is with the Gini of the ORF-wide mRNA structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The linear sequences of bacterial mRNAs encode not only ORFs, but also ORF-wide secondary structures.
source: In toto, these analyses indicate that the linear sequences of bacterial mRNAs encode not only ORFs, but also ORF-wide secondary structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the various correlation analyses.

claim: ORF-wide secondary structures provide a rough blueprint for the TE of that ORF.
source: These structures provide a rough blueprint for the TE of that ORF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between structure and TE.

claim: Instructions from the structural blueprint are augmented by ribosomes and additional factors.
source: Instructions from this blueprint are augmented by ribosomes and additional factors (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that correlation increases with translation.

claim: The strength of the Shine-Dalgarno sequence does not have predictive power for TE, even after controlling for structure as measured by Gini index.
source: Consistent with earlier studies (Li et al., 2014), we found that the strength of the Shine-Dalgarno sequence does not have predictive power for TE, even after controlling for structure as measured by Gini index (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Codon usage, quantified by tAI, modestly correlates with TE (ρ = 0.34).
source: Codon usage, quantified by tAI (tRNA adaptation index) (dos Reis et al., 2004; Tuller et al., 2010) modestly correlates with TE (ρ = 0.34, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Codon usage correlates more strongly with the overall rate of translation (ρ = 0.61) than with TE.
source: Interestingly, codon usage correlates more strongly with the overall rate of translation (i.e. average ribosome footprint density, ρ = 0.61) and ORF mRNA abundance (RPKM of mRNA sequencing, ρ = 0.48) than with their TE's (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Codon usage correlates with ORF mRNA abundance (ρ = 0.48).
source: Interestingly, codon usage correlates more strongly with the overall rate of translation (i.e. average ribosome footprint density, ρ = 0.61) and ORF mRNA abundance (RPKM of mRNA sequencing, ρ = 0.48) than with their TE's (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: The Gini score exhibits its highest correlation with TE (ρ = −0.76) and is poorly correlated with mRNA abundance (ρ = −0.05).
source: In contrast, the Gini score exhibits its highest correlation with TE (ρ = −0.76, Figure 3C) and is poorly correlated with mRNA abundance (ρ = −0.05) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Codon bias may be evolutionally selected to correspond to the ORF expression level rather than to its translation efficiency.
source: This suggests that codon bias may be evolutionally selected to correspond to the ORF expression level rather than to its translation efficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that codon usage correlates better with expression level than with TE.

claim: Codon usage correlates with mRNA half-life in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes.
source: Additionally, there is evidence that codon usage correlates with mRNA half-life in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes (Boël et al., 2016; Presnyak et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boël et al., 2016 and Presnyak et al., 2015.

claim: ORF-wide codon usage (tAI) and intrinsic mRNA structure are largely independent variables.
source: ORF-wide codon usage (tAI) and intrinsic mRNA structure appear to be largely independent variables, as they show little correlation with each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The codon influence metric is relatively weakly correlated with TE under physiological conditions for endogenous genes (ρ = 0.29).
source: Although a novel metric quantifying codon influence was highly successful at predicting protein production from overexpressed exogenous genes transcribed by T7 RNA polymerase (Boël et al., 2016), it is relatively weakly correlated with TE under physiological conditions for endogenous genes (ρ = 0.29) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 4D and citation to Boël et al., 2016.

claim: The codons providing efficient translation of an over-expressed transgene may differ from the efficient codons for an endogenous gene.
source: This suggests that the codons providing efficient translation of an over-expressed transgene may differ from the efficient codons for an endogenous gene, as overexpression causes amino acid starvation and concomitant alteration of charged tRNA pools (Plotkin and Kudla, 2011; Welch et al., 2009; Dittmar et al., 2005; Elf et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the weak correlation of codon influence with endogenous TE and supported by citations.

claim: ORF-wide mRNA secondary structure is by far the strongest and most significant predictor of endogenous TE compared to other factors.
source: Overall, ORF-wide mRNA secondary structure is by far the strongest and most significant predictor of endogenous TE compared to the other factors discussed above (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A linear regression model that includes the Boel metric, tAI, and Shine-Dalgarno sequence strength showed marginal improvement in predictive power compared to ORF-wide structure alone.
source: A linear regression model that includes the addition of the Boel metric, tAI, and Shine-Dalgarno sequence strength showed marginal improvement in the predictive power compared to the ORF-wide structure alone (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the regression analysis mentioned.

claim: Codon optimization may be critical for highly expressed genes due to higher demand for these tRNAs and may play a role in setting the appropriate mRNA half-life.
source: Therefore, rather than being a driver for TE, codon optimization may be critical for highly expressed genes due to higher demand for these tRNAs and may play a role in setting the appropriate mRNA half-life.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that codon usage correlates with expression level rather than TE.

claim: Overexpressed transgenes are likely to perturb the balance between codon usage and tRNA abundance, creating a global translation defect.
source: Considering the fact that the expression of each tRNA species is tuned to the endogenous usage of its cognate codon(s) (Dong et al., 1996), overexpressed transgenes are likely to perturb the balance between codon usage and tRNA abundance, creating a global translation defect (Shah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between tRNA expression and codon usage, supported by citations.

claim: When the minimal ORF contains the rare leucine codon CUA, elevated ribosome occupancy at CUA codons in endogenous genes is observed.
source: When the minimal ORF contains the rare leucine codon CUA, which has only one cognate tRNA, we observed elevated ribosome occupancy at CUA codons in endogenous genes (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Slow translation at CUA codons in the leuL leader sequence triggers the expression of leucine biosynthetic genes.
source: In particular, slow translation at CUA codons in the leuL leader sequence triggers the expression of leucine biosynthetic genes (Figure 4H)
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Overexpressing the minimal ORF with the common leucine codon CUG does not change the expression level or ribosome occupancy at leucine codons of endogenous genes.
source: whereas overexpressing the minimal ORF with the common leucine codon CUG or without any coding sequence does not change the expression level or ribosome occupancy at leucine codons of endogenous genes (Figure 4G and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 4G and 4I.

claim: Overexpression of a rare codon can deplete the pool of free cognate aa-tRNA molecules, leading to global perturbation of translation.
source: These results suggest that overexpression of a rare codon and not a common codon can deplete the pool of free cognate aa-tRNA molecules, leading to global perturbation of translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing effects of rare codon overexpression.

claim: Cells expressing a transgene that contain more rare codons are under a different physiological state compared to WT cells solely expressing endogenous genes.
source: Cells expressing a transgene that contain more rare codons are thus under a different physiological state compared to WT cells solely expressing endogenous genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rare codon overexpression perturbs translation.

claim: The majority of adjacent ORFs (62%) are separated by only 25nt or less.
source: Bacterial operons are densely packed with ORFs, as the majority of adjacent ORFs (62%) are separated by only 25nt or less (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cumulative distribution data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: mRNA structure undergoes a sharp transition at ORF boundaries.
source: Our finding that ORF mRNAs have a roughly similar degree of structure (Gini index) throughout their entire length (Figure 2A–D), but that the degree of structure of adjacent ORF mRNAs on polycistronic transcripts can differ significantly (Figure 2G) suggests that mRNA structure undergoes a sharp transition at ORF boundaries.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORFs have consistent internal structure but differ from adjacent ORFs.

claim: Local degree of mRNA folding immediately downstream of the start site correlates with the TE of the downstream gene.
source: We find that the local degree of mRNA folding immediately downstream of the start site correlates with the TE of the downstream gene, but that this correlation rapidly diminishes upstream of the start site.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Local mRNA structure upstream of the start site is only correlated with the TE of the upstream ORF.
source: Conversely, local mRNA structure upstream of the start site is only correlated with the TE of the upstream ORF (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Polycistronic mRNAs consist of distinct ORF-length structural domains.
source: Thus, mRNA structure undergoes a sharp transition at ORF boundaries, and polycistronic mRNAs consist of distinct ORF-length structural domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis at ORF boundaries.

claim: There is a lack of structure in the immediate vicinity of the start sites for most ORFs.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Eyre-Walker and Bulmer, 1993; Scharff et al., 2011; Bentele et al., 2013; Del Campo et al., 2015), we found a lack of structure in the immediate vicinity of the start sites for most ORFs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5E and citations to previous studies.

claim: Downstream from the structure-free zone (25–50 nt), endogenous mRNA has a high propensity to base pair with regions further downstream within the same ORF.
source: Downstream from this structure-free zone (25–50 nt), endogenous mRNA has a high propensity to base pair with regions further downstream, that is pairing within the same ORF (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the directionality analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Nucleotides located 25-50nt upstream of the start site have a strong preference for interacting with regions further upstream in the preceding ORF.
source: Conversely, nucleotides located 25-50nt upstream of the start site have a strong preference for interacting with regions further upstream in the preceding ORF (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the directionality analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The sharp transition in the directionality of base-pairing around start sites is driven by the mRNA sequence itself.
source: Importantly, in vivo mRNA without translating ribosomes and in vitro probed mRNA (Figure 5E–F) also showed such preferences. Thus, the sharp transition in the directionality of base-pairing around start sites is driven by the mRNA sequence itself, promoting ORF-centric units of secondary structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the directionality preference persists without translation.

claim: The dusB-M3 mutation decreases Fis expression.
source: Previous work indicated that the upstream dusB gene has a stem-loop structure near the 3' end of the gene; that mutationally disrupting the stem-loop (Mutation M3; Figure 6A) decreased translation of fis; and that restoring base pairing by a second mutation (M2) restored fis translation for unknown reasons (Nafissi et al., 2012). After confirming these results (Figure 6B)
evidence: This claim is supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 6B and citation to Nafissi et al., 2012.

claim: The complementary M2 mutation rescues Fis expression in the dusB-M3 mutant.
source: and that restoring base pairing by a second mutation (M2) restored fis translation for unknown reasons (Nafissi et al., 2012). After confirming these results (Figure 6B)
evidence: This claim is supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 6B and citation to Nafissi et al., 2012.

claim: In the M3 mutant, the -58 ~ −53nt region pairs with the +9 ~ +14 nt region of fis, rather than forming a stem-loop structure within dusB.
source: In the M3 mutant, the -58 ~ −53nt region (blue) pairs with the +9 ~ +14 nt region of fis (red), rather than forming a stem-loop structure within dusB as it does in WT and M3:2 cells (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural predictions shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: The increased structure of fis mRNA in the M3 mutant starts at the ORF boundary and spreads across the entire downstream coding region of fis.
source: The increased structure of fis mRNA in the M3 mutant starts at the ORF boundary and spreads across the entire downstream coding region of fis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutation M3 induces long-range interactions between mRNA of the dusB and fis ORFs, which are normally structurally insulated from each other.
source: Thus, mutation M3 induces long-range interactions between mRNA of the dusB and fis ORFs, which are normally structurally insulated from each other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis of the M3 mutant.

claim: Specific sequences isolate mRNA folding within adjacent ORFs thereby minimizing structural crosstalk between adjacent ORFs.
source: In toto, our results suggest that specific sequences isolate mRNA folding within adjacent ORFs thereby minimizing structural crosstalk between adjacent ORFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dusB-fis mutational analysis.

claim: Disruption of structural boundaries affects both local and long-range mRNA folding.
source: Disruption of structural boundaries affects both local and long-range mRNA folding, which is likely to be critical for programming the degree of translational isolation between ORFs on the same mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of the M3 mutation on fis structure.

claim: Polycistronic mRNAs are organized into ORF-centric modules with characteristic but different extents of mRNA structure, punctuated by regions of low basepairing close to the translational start site.
source: Polycistronic mRNAs are organized into ORF-centric modules with characteristic but different extents of mRNA structure, punctuated by regions of low basepairing close to the translational start site (A).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The intrinsic ORF-wide mRNA structure is highly predictive of translation efficiency.
source: The intrinsic ORF-wide mRNA structure is highly predictive of translation efficiency (B)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Intrinsic mRNA structure is amplified by translation, in a self-reinforcing loop, to provide the mRNA structure that ultimately specifies the translation of each ORF in an operon.
source: and is amplified by translation, in a self-reinforcing loop, to provide the mRNA structure that ultimately specifies the translation of each ORF in an operon.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion shown in Figure 7.

claim: E. coli K-12 MG1655 was used as the WT strain.
source: E. coli K-12 MG1655 (RRID:SCR_002433) was used as the WT strain.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: All culture experiments were performed in MOPS medium supplemented with 0.2% glucose, all amino acids except methionine, vitamins, bases and micronutrients.
source: All culture experiments were performed in MOPS medium supplemented with 0.2% glucose, all amino acids except methionine, vitamins, bases and micronutrients (Teknova, Hollister CA).
evidence: This is a methodological statement.
